violations.message: expected real return 1.51% is below the CPI + 3.0% target
ex-ante tracking error 9.27% exceeds the 6.0% budget vs. 60/40 equity-bond benchmark

body.rationale:
HRP uses no expected returns and never inverts the covariance matrix. It orders assets by a single-linkage dendrogram on correlation distance, then splits risk budgets recursively in inverse proportion to cluster variance. It cannot inherit CMA error, and it cannot blow up on a near-singular matrix the way maximum Sharpe does. In an expansion regime, where return forecasts are noisy and dispersed, that is a defensible stance, and it is the kind of covariance-driven argument §4.3 found persuasive.

The concentration here is the method working as designed, not a failure. Cash is a 0.6%-volatility asset, and HRP's recursion hands it nearly all the budget because it sits in its own cluster with far lower variance than anything else. The 1.4 effective assets and 0.848 Herfindahl follow directly. HRP is not finding a clever diversification. It is reporting that, on covariance alone and with no IPS floor on risk, almost any risk-based allocation collapses into cash. A reviewer should read this as a diagnostic of the opportunity set, not as a view on cash.

The portfolio is far outside the IPS, and I will not dress that up. Volatility is 0.65% against an 8-12% band, tracking error is 9.27% against a 6% budget, and expected real return of 1.51% is below CPI + 3%. All three are hard breaches, and the draft IPS is only provisional. HRP has no parameter that moves it toward the band without becoming a different method, so I propose it as it is. The breach is structural, not a tuning accident.

What it offers a compliant ensemble is a risk-ordered, estimation-error-free anchor. The CIO can use it as the low-risk, return-agnostic component, blended with return-aware or equity-heavy proposals that supply the return and volatility the IPS needs. Its dendrogram also shows which assets cluster together (for example the Treasury and credit blocks), which is useful to a CIO deciding how to split budgets. The paper's CIO weighted portfolios that breached on their own, and this is that kind of input. On its own it fails the mandate. I am not arguing for holding it alone.
body.notes: Key assumption: Asset risk is adequately described by the historical covariance and its correlation hierarchy, and low realised volatility is a reliable proxy for low risk going forward. Under this, a risk budget should go in inverse proportion to cluster variance, with no information from expected returns. Main weakness: The portfolio is about 92% cash and fails three hard IPS limits: 0.65% volatility, 9.27% tracking error, and a 1.51% real return below the CPI + 3% target. HRP has no return or risk-target mechanism, so it will always collapse into the lowest-variance asset when one exists. It gives up the return needed to meet the mandate, which makes it unusable standalone. Its Sharpe of 0.14 is also weak, because the judged CMAs it ignores put cash's return well below what risk-taking assets offer. Preferred when: When expected-return forecasts are unreliable or untrusted, covariance is better estimated than means, and the matrix is ill-conditioned enough to make inversion-based methods unstable. It also fits as a capital-preservation or defensive sleeve inside an ensemble, where another component supplies the return and the IPS volatility target. It is the wrong choice as the CIO's standalone recommendation under this IPS. Invalidated if: The case fails if the CMAs prove reliable enough that return-aware methods earn their estimation error, if cash's low volatility is not a durable property (for instance a rate shock or inflation that erodes its real return, which the 1.51% real return hints at), or if correlations shift so that the dendrogram clusters no longer hold. It is also the wrong choice whenever the IPS volatility band and the CPI + 3% return target are binding for the final recommendation, since a standalone 92% cash allocation cannot meet either.
